request.prompt: Scene: the potting room, far view. The camera stands in the north-east corner of the garden on the gravel path, eight blocks from the potting room, at eye height, facing north-west, looking at the small red brick potting room from its front-right corner, at dusk after the sun has gone: the sky deep blue with a last band of gold low on the left. NOT looking along the pool. The potting room fills the centre: red brick walls, a tiled roof, an oak plank door standing ajar with warm light spilling out onto the path, a small window glowing with lantern and candle light. Behind it the tall north wall; at the left edge the end of the glass conservatory. Two lantern posts along the path in the foreground, lit.
request.style_note: The Glasshouse, an old walled kitchen garden on a quiet upland shelf, with a white-framed glass conservatory standing against its north wall, a small brick potting room beside it and a stone terrace on its west wall looking out over a wide open valley, drawn in the same hand throughout: warm painterly concept painting at golden hour, the sun low and setting in the west, long soft shadows, a clear sky shading from deep blue overhead to pale gold and rose at the horizon, warm red brick walls with pale stone copings, honey-coloured oak planks, grey cobblestone and pale gravel paths, fresh green lawn, clipped dark-green hedges, round fruit trees in leaf, white-painted wooden glazing bars on clear glass, still water mirroring the sky, small warm accents of lantern and candle light, crisp readable silhouettes. Everything is massed from large squared blocks with flat faces and clean right angles so every form could be built block by block in Minecraft: walls are coursed brick in whole blocks, the trees are chunky cubic masses of leaves on square trunks, the glass is flat square panes in a grid of white frames, roofs are stepped. The garden is a real, lived-in working garden, tidy and loved. No person appears unless the view names one, and then only an ordinary older woman in a gardener's apron. Each image is ONE single full-frame view of that place, filling the frame edge to edge: never a sheet, never a grid, never a panel, never an inset, never a caption, label, text or border.
